```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
from coreforecast.scalers import boxcox, boxcox_lambda

from coursekit import datasets as D
from coursekit import plotting as P

P.use_course_style()

spine = D.spine()
beer = D.beer()
souvenirs = D.souvenirs()
noise = D.white_noise(n=len(spine), seed=7)

_stl_raw = STL(spine["y"].to_numpy(), period=12, robust=True).fit()
trend_only = spine.assign(y=np.asarray(_stl_raw.trend))
season_only = spine.assign(
    y=np.asarray(_stl_raw.seasonal) + np.asarray(_stl_raw.resid)
)
```

## Beyond visual inspection

Describing patterns by eye has 3 fatal flaws:

::: {.incremental}
- **Does not scale** — impossible across hundreds of series
- **Subjective** — different people see different patterns
- **No significance test** — cannot tell signal from noise
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Solution
Replace guesswork with **numerical diagnostics**: ACF, STL decomposition, and feature summaries.
:::

# A. Autocorrelation {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 2.8–2.9 · The central diagnostic

## A lag plot on a trending series only shows the trend

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
detrended = spine["y"].to_numpy() - P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 4.4))
P.lag_plot_grid(spine["y"], lags=(1, 6, 12), axes=axes[0])
P.lag_plot_grid(pd.Series(detrended).dropna(), lags=(1, 6, 12), axes=axes[1])
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("raw turnover ($M)", size=10)
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("trend removed ($M)", size=10)
plt.show()
```

::: {.incremental}
- Raw (top): every lag scores $r \approx 0.98$, which is the trend talking
- Trend removed (bottom): lag 12 jumps to $0.73$, lag 6 turns **negative**
:::

::: {.notes}
The trend is removed here with a 12-month moving average, which is segment 4. Do not
teach it yet. The point is only that the raw lag plot cannot separate the two.
:::

## Autocorrelation ($r_k$)

Quantifies linear correlation between $y_t$ and its lag $y_{t-k}$:

$$r_k = \frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}(y_t - \bar{y})(y_{t-k} - \bar{y})}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t - \bar{y})^2}$$

::: {.incremental}
- **$r_k \in [-1, 1]$**
- **$r_1$** $\rightarrow$ correlation with previous month (inertia/trend)
- **$r_{12}$** $\rightarrow$ correlation with same month last year (seasonality)
:::

::: {.notes}
Standard sample correlation between the series and itself shifted by k steps.
:::

## The Correlogram (ACF Plot)

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.2))
P.acf_plot(spine["y"], nlags=36, ax=ax, highlight_every=12,
           title="Spine ACF — 36 Lags (Annual spikes in orange)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Dashed blue lines indicate **95% significance bounds** ($\pm 1.96 / \sqrt{T}$).
:::

## Significance Bounds

If a series is pure white noise:

$$r_k \sim N\left(0,\ \tfrac{1}{T}\right)$$

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- 95% of autocorrelations fall inside **$\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}$**
- A spike inside the bounds is indistinguishable from noise
- With 36 lags, ~1–2 spikes outside the bounds can occur by chance
:::

## Three distinct ACF signatures

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10.5, 5.4))

P.plot_series(trend_only, ax=axes[0, 0], title="Trend only")
P.plot_series(season_only, ax=axes[0, 1], title="Seasonality only", color=P.BLUE)
P.plot_series(noise, ax=axes[0, 2], title="White noise", color=P.GREY)
for ax in axes[0]:
    ax.set_xlabel("")

P.acf_plot(trend_only["y"], nlags=36, ax=axes[1, 0], title="Slow decay")
P.acf_plot(season_only["y"], nlags=36, ax=axes[1, 1], highlight_every=12,
           color=P.BLUE, title="Spikes at 12, 24, 36")
P.acf_plot(noise["y"], nlags=36, ax=axes[1, 2], color=P.GREY,
           title="All inside bounds")
P.thin_xticks(axes[0], n=3)
plt.show()
```

## How to interpret any ACF

| Visual Pattern | Underlying Property |
|---|---|
| Slow, smooth decay | **Trend** |
| Repeating peaks at $m, 2m, 3m$ | **Seasonality** (period $m$) |
| Decay + Seasonal peaks | **Trend + Seasonality** |
| All spikes inside bounds | **White Noise** (no remaining signal) |

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
**Key application**: When model residuals are white noise, the model has captured all systematic structure.
:::

# B. Decomposition {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 3 · Separating trend, season, and noise

## 1. Stabilise the variance (Box-Cox)

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
lam = boxcox_lambda(spine["y"].to_numpy(), method="loglik")
yt = boxcox(spine["y"].to_numpy(), lam)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
P.plot_series(spine, ax=axes[0], title="Original — Expanding swing")
axes[1].plot(spine["ds"], yt, color=P.ORANGE, lw=0.9)
axes[1].set_title(rf"Box-Cox ($\lambda = {lam:.2f}$) — Constant swing")
plt.show()
```

::: {.incremental}
- When swing grows with level, transform before decomposing
- $\lambda \approx 0 \implies$ Use a standard **log transform** ($\log y_t$)
:::

## A centred moving average estimates the trend-cycle

$$\hat{T}_t = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} y_{t+j} \qquad (m = 2k + 1)$$

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.5))
P.trend_overlay_plot(
    spine, {"3-MA": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 3),
            "2×12-MA": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12)},
    ax=ax, tail=180, colors=[P.PINK, P.ORANGE], ylabel="turnover ($M)",
    title="Spine, last 15 years: the order $m$ decides what survives")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Most common use of a centred moving average: **estimating the trend-cycle of
seasonal data**. $m = 3$ keeps the season, $m = 12$ erases it.
:::

## The season cancels because the window is one whole cycle

Take $y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t$, where $S_t$ has period $m$ and one full cycle sums
to zero (the usual identifying constraint):

$$\sum_{j=0}^{m-1} S_{t+j} = 0$$

. . .

Averaging $m = 2k+1$ terms centred on $t$ splits into three pieces:

$$\hat{T}_t = \underbrace{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} T_{t+j}}_{\text{trend}}
            + \underbrace{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} S_{t+j}}_{\text{season}}
            + \underbrace{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} R_{t+j}}_{\text{noise}}$$

## Season deleted, trend kept, noise damped

::: {.incremental}
- **Season $= 0$, exactly.** The window spans one whole cycle, so that sum *is*
  the constraint above. Nothing approximate about it.
- **Trend survives.** If $T_{t+j} \approx a + bj$ locally, then
  $\frac{1}{m}\sum_j (a + bj) = a = T_t$, because $\sum_{j=-k}^{k} j = 0$.
  A symmetric window is **unbiased on a linear trend**.
- **Noise shrinks.** $\operatorname{Var}(\bar{R}) = \sigma^2 / m$: damped by
  averaging, never removed.
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
What is left is a trend-cycle estimate.
:::

## An even $m$ needs the 2×$m$-MA to stay centred

Twelve consecutive months have **no middle month**, so their average sits at
$t + \tfrac{1}{2}$. Average two adjacent 12-MAs to land back on $t$:

$$\hat{T}_t = \tfrac{1}{24}y_{t-6} + \tfrac{1}{12}\sum_{j=-5}^{5} y_{t+j}
              + \tfrac{1}{24}y_{t+6}$$

```{python}
#| fig-width: 7.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 1.5))
P.ma_weight_plot(12, ax=ax, title="13 weights, symmetric about $t$")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .teal}
$y_{t-6}$ and $y_{t+6}$ are the **same calendar month**, so between them they
carry $\tfrac{1}{12}$, like every other month. The season still cancels exactly.
:::

## Classical decomposition is that MA plus monthly means

::: {.incremental}
1. $\hat{T}_t$ is the 2×12-MA
2. Detrend: $y_t - \hat{T}_t$
3. $\hat{S}$ averages the detrended values within each month, then centres them
   to sum to zero
4. $\hat{R}_t = y_t - \hat{T}_t - \hat{S}_t$
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
Every piece is a moving average or a group mean. No fitting, no parameters. That
simplicity costs something.
:::

## The MA trend stops six months short of the present

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.3))
P.trend_overlay_plot(
    spine, {"2×12-MA trend": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12),
            "STL trend": trend_only["y"].to_numpy()},
    ax=ax, tail=60, colors=[P.ORANGE, P.BLUE], shade_gap="2×12-MA trend",
    ylabel="turnover ($M)", title="Spine, last 5 years")
plt.show()
```

::: {.incremental}
- The first and last $m/2$ observations get no trend estimate, and the last one
  is exactly where you forecast from
- Monthly means impose one seasonal shape on all 37 years
:::

## 3. STL Decomposition

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
res = STL(yt, period=12, robust=True).fit()
dcmp = spine.assign(
    transformed=yt,
    trend=np.asarray(res.trend),
    seasonal=np.asarray(res.seasonal),
    remainder=np.asarray(res.resid),
)
fig, axes = P.decomposition_plot(
    dcmp, ["transformed", "trend", "seasonal", "remainder"],
    "STL Decomposition (Transformed Spine)")
plt.show()
```

## Why STL works well

::: {.incremental}
- **Adaptive** — seasonal pattern can evolve smoothly over time
- **Flexible trend** — estimates non-linear trend curves
- **Robust** — outliers do not distort the trend (`robust=True`)
- **Remainder** — isolates pure unexplained variation
:::

::: {.notes}
STL = Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess. Key parameters: period (must provide) and seasonal window.
:::

## Seasonally Adjusted Series

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.2))
ax.plot(spine["ds"], dcmp["transformed"], color=P.GREY, lw=0.8, label="Observed")
ax.plot(spine["ds"], dcmp["transformed"] - dcmp["seasonal"], color=P.ORANGE,
        lw=1.2, label="Seasonally adjusted")
ax.set(title="Observed vs. Seasonally Adjusted ($y_t - S_t$)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .navy}
Removing seasonality reveals true economic shifts (e.g. 2008 downturn).
:::

# C. Time Series Features {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #9B8EC0)"}

Ch 4 · Summarising thousands of series

## The portfolio scaling problem

::: {.incremental}
- In practice, you manage **hundreds or thousands** of series
- Manual visual inspection is impossible
- Solution: Compute summary **features** (1 row per series)
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
A **feature** is a numerical summary of a whole series (e.g. trend strength, seasonal strength, entropy).
:::

## Strength of Trend & Seasonality

Using STL component variances:

$$F_T = \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(T_t + R_t)}\right) \qquad F_S = \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(S_t + R_t)}\right)$$

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Values fall strictly in **$[0, 1]$**
- **$F_T \approx 0$** $\rightarrow$ No trend | **$F_T \approx 1$** $\rightarrow$ Strong trend
- **$F_S \approx 0$** $\rightarrow$ No seasonality | **$F_S \approx 1$** $\rightarrow$ Strong seasonality
:::

## 148 retail series mapped in 2D

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9.5
def stl_features(g):
    y = np.log(np.clip(g["y"].to_numpy(), 1e-6, None))
    r = STL(y, period=12, robust=True).fit()
    R, T_, S = np.asarray(r.resid), np.asarray(r.trend), np.asarray(r.seasonal)
    vr = np.var(R)
    return pd.Series({
        "trend_strength": max(0.0, 1 - vr / np.var(T_ + R)),
        "seasonal_strength": max(0.0, 1 - vr / np.var(S + R)),
        "n": len(g),
    })

allr = D.retail_all()
feat = (allr.groupby("unique_id")[["y"]]
             .apply(stl_features, include_groups=False)
             .reset_index())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.6))
ax.scatter(feat["trend_strength"], feat["seasonal_strength"], s=26,
           color=P.BLUE, alpha=0.6)
lo = feat.nsmallest(1, "seasonal_strength").iloc[0]
hi = feat.nlargest(1, "seasonal_strength").iloc[0]
mine = feat[feat["unique_id"] == D.SPINE_ID].iloc[0]
for row, col in [(lo, P.GREY), (hi, P.ORANGE), (mine, P.GREEN)]:
    ax.scatter([row["trend_strength"]], [row["seasonal_strength"]], s=110,
               color=col, zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(row["unique_id"], (row["trend_strength"], row["seasonal_strength"]),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-10, 8), size=9, color=col,
                ha="right")
ax.set(xlabel="Trend Strength ($F_T$)", ylabel="Seasonal Strength ($F_S$)",
       title="Australian Retail Portfolio Feature Map")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Notice all retail series have FT > 0.96. Trend strength does not discriminate in this portfolio; seasonal strength provides the separation.
:::

## Practical uses of feature maps

::: {.incremental}
- **Triage** — focus manual attention on unusual series
- **Model Routing** — skip seasonal models if $F_S \approx 0$
- **Anomaly Detection** — feature outliers often indicate data errors
- **Clustering** — group similar series for global models
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## Golden Rule
When a point looks anomalous in feature space, **always plot the raw series**.
:::
